assertions.before: **Bankruptcy armor (multi-member).** Article 11 of the multi-member agreement declares the agreement an executory contract under 11 U.S.C. §365, catalogs each member's material ongoing duties, and — citing *In re Soderstrom* (M.D. Fla. 2013) — takes the position that a bankruptcy trustee cannot assume or assign a debtor-member's interest without the other members' consent. Understand it honestly: bankruptcy courts wield broad equitable power, and no drafting guarantees an outcome there. Article 11 gives your side the strongest available argument; combined with charging-order exclusivity, it makes the interest an unappetizing target — which is the practical goal.
assertions.after: **Bankruptcy armor (multi-member).** Article 11 describes the members' continuing managerial and governance obligations and states that the agreement is intended to be an executory contract under 11 U.S.C. §365. Section 11.2 requires the other members' prior written consent before a bankruptcy trustee or debtor in possession may assume or assign a debtor-member's governance or management rights, or cause a substitute to be admitted as a member, under §365(c)(1) and applicable Florida law. This separates control of the company from the economic interest: the section does not limit the bankruptcy estate's interest in the debtor-member's transferable economic interest to the extent permitted by applicable law. It is not a promise that economic rights cannot enter the estate or be sold. The provision's effect depends on applicable law and the bankruptcy court's decision; no drafting guarantees an outcome.

assertions.before: Article 11 is bankruptcy armor. It frames the agreement as a contract with ongoing, unperformed duties owed by every member — capital calls (if §6.2 is included), participation in governance, noncompetition (if Alternative A is selected), confidentiality, and non-disparagement — and, citing Florida bankruptcy precedent, takes the position that a bankruptcy trustee for one member cannot take over or sell that member's interest without the other members' consent. Together with the charging-order provision (§10.6), it is designed to keep a co-owner's personal bankruptcy or judgment creditor from putting a stranger in your company.
assertions.after: Article 11 describes the members' continuing obligations — capital calls (if §6.2 is included), participation in governance, noncompetition (if Alternative A is selected), confidentiality, and non-disparagement — and states that the agreement is intended to be an executory contract. Section 11.2 requires the other members' prior written consent before a bankruptcy trustee or debtor in possession may assume or assign a debtor-member's governance or management rights, or cause a substitute to be admitted as a member, under 11 U.S.C. §365(c)(1) and applicable Florida law. The section distinguishes those rights from the member's transferable economic interest: it does not limit the estate's interest in those economic rights to the extent permitted by applicable law.
